short: The speech of Allah revealed to Muhammad in Arabic over about twenty three years, preserved word for word.
long: The word means the recitation, from a root meaning to read aloud. It is one book of 114 surahs, revealed piece by piece between Makkah and Madinah, memorised by the Companions and written down in the Prophet's lifetime. Muslims hold that the Arabic wording is itself the revelation, which is why any rendering into another language is called a translation of the meaning and never the Qur'an.

short: The family of disciplines that study how the Qur'an was revealed, collected, recited, read and interpreted.
long: It covers revelation and its occasions, Makkan and Madinan passages, the canonical readings, abrogation, the clear and the ambiguous, and the rules of interpretation. It is the map you are meant to have before opening a work of tafsir. The two classic reference works are al-Zarkashi's al-Burhan and al-Suyuti's al-Itqan.

short: A physical copy of the Qur'an: the pages, ink and binding, as distinct from the revelation itself.
long: The word comes from sahifah, a written sheet, so a mushaf is the sheets gathered between two covers. Muslims keep the distinction: the Qur'an is the speech of Allah, the mushaf is the object you can drop or tear. Worn out copies are not put in the bin; they are buried or burned in a clean place. Uthman burned the copies his standard edition replaced, and later scholars differ over which of the two is better.

short: A verse of the Qur'an, and in ordinary Arabic a sign.
long: The same word is used for the signs of Allah in creation, which is why a verse is called a sign rather than a line. Most scholars hold that verse endings were fixed by the Prophet's own recitation; the numbers printed in the margins were added later as an aid. The Hafs printing counts 6,236 verses, and other counting traditions divide a few verses differently and reach slightly different totals.

short: A chapter of the Qur'an; there are 114, arranged in the mushaf rather than by date of revelation.
long: Each surah has a name, usually taken from a striking word inside it, and every surah except at-Tawbah opens with the basmalah. They range from al-Baqarah at 286 verses down to al-Kawthar at three. The order in the mushaf is not the order of revelation, so many of the short surahs at the end are among the earliest to come down.

short: One of the thirty roughly equal parts the Qur'an is divided into, for reading it over a month.
long: The division is a reading aid rather than part of the revelation, and it usually cuts across a surah rather than falling neatly between two. In South Asia a juz is called a para or sipara. Reading one juz a day completes the whole Qur'an in a month, which is why almost every Ramadan schedule is built on it.

short: The thirtieth and last part of the Qur'an, running from Surah an-Naba to the end.
long: It is named after its first word, amma, in the opening verse of an-Naba. It holds thirty seven short surahs, the ones most used in prayer, so it is where children and new Muslims usually begin memorising. Small printed booklets of it are sold everywhere for exactly that reason.

short: Half a juz; the Qur'an is divided into sixty hizbs for steady daily reading.
long: The word means a share or portion, in the sense of a person's allotted reading. Each hizb is split again into four quarters, marked in the margin of most mushafs. In parts of North and West Africa the daily recitation of a mosque is organised around the hizb rather than the juz.

short: A quarter of a hizb, shown by the small ornamental star in the margin of the mushaf.
long: There are 240 of these quarters, four to each of the sixty hizbs. The symbol is a printer's mark added by later scholars so readers can keep their place and portion out a daily amount. It carries no ruling; nothing is said or done when you reach one.

short: One of seven divisions of the Qur'an, used by those who complete a full reading each week.
long: Companions are reported to have divided their reading this way, in portions of three, five, seven, nine, eleven and thirteen surahs, with the remainder of the mushaf as the seventh. It is an older habit than the thirty part division and is still followed by some. A separate booklet of protective verses is also called Manzil; it borrowed the name but is a different thing.

short: A short thematic passage marked with a small ain in the margin, mostly in South Asian mushafs.
long: The word is the same one used for bowing in prayer, because an imam would recite one such passage and then bow. It groups a handful of verses that hang together, which makes it a natural unit for tarawih and for memorising. It is a later reading aid and is absent from most Arab printings.

short: The last stretch of the Qur'an, from about Surah Qaf to the end, made up of shorter surahs.
long: The name means the frequently divided, because the basmalah separates its many short surahs so often. Scholars split it into long, middle and short sections, which is the language books of fiqh use when describing what to recite in each prayer. Where it begins is disputed: most say Surah Qaf, others say al-Hujurat.

short: The single letters that open twenty nine surahs, such as Alif Lam Mim, recited letter by letter.
long: They are read as separate letter names, not run together as a word. Many early scholars, Companions among them, said their meaning is known to Allah alone and stopped there. Others suggested they point at the challenge itself: this revelation is built from the very letters its opponents already had.

short: The seven verse opening surah, recited in the prayer; most schools require it in every unit.
long: Its names include the Opening, the Mother of the Book, and the seven oft repeated verses. It is a prayer spoken in the second person: praise first, then a single request, for guidance on the straight path. The schools differ over whether the basmalah counts as its first verse, which is why the seven verses are numbered differently in different mushafs. They differ again over whether someone praying behind an imam recites it: the Hanafis hold that the imam's recitation stands for him.

short: The opening line In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful, found before nearly every surah.
long: It stands at the head of 113 surahs; at-Tawbah alone has none. It also appears inside the Qur'an as the opening of Sulayman's letter in Surah an-Naml. The schools differ over whether it is a verse of al-Fatihah and whether it is said aloud in prayer, which is why practice varies from one mosque to the next.

short: Saying I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Shaytan before beginning to recite.
long: The Qur'an instructs it directly: when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge with Allah from Shaytan the rejected. It is said once at the start of a sitting, not before every verse, and it is not itself part of the Qur'an. Most scholars treat it as strongly recommended rather than obligatory.

short: The phrase Allah the Magnificent has spoken the truth, often said on finishing a recitation.
long: The words are true in themselves and echo a phrase in Surah Al Imran. What scholars differ over is treating them as a fixed ending that must always follow recitation, since neither the Prophet nor the early generations are known to have made a habit of it. Some call it a harmless custom, others discourage making it a rule; leaving it out is not a fault.

short: A verse or surah revealed before the migration to Madinah, whatever place it came down in.
long: The usual definition is by time rather than geography, so a verse revealed at Makkah during the farewell pilgrimage still counts as Madani. Makki passages tend to be shorter and more urgent, dealing with belief, resurrection and the earlier prophets, and often open with O mankind. Around eighty six surahs are classed as Makki, with several disputed.

short: A verse or surah revealed after the migration to Madinah, whatever place it came down in.
long: Madani passages generally deal with the shape of a community: law, family, treaties, warfare, hypocrisy and the People of the Book, and they often open with O you who believe. Their verses are usually longer. Around twenty eight surahs are classed as Madani, and for a few the classification is contested or mixed.

short: The sending down of the Qur'an: gradually, over roughly twenty three years, alongside real events.
long: The first revelation was Iqra, in the cave of Hira, and the last verses came near the end of the Prophet's life. The Qur'an explains its own slow pace: it came in stages to steady the Prophet's heart. A well known report from Ibn Abbas adds an earlier stage, the whole Qur'an brought down to the lowest heaven on Laylat al-Qadr and then released piece by piece.

short: The event or question a particular verse was revealed in answer to.
long: Knowing the occasion often makes a verse click into place, and it guards against reading a narrow ruling as a sweeping one. These occasions reach us only through narrations, so they are weighed like any report, and a great many verses have no occasion attached at all. The working rule for most scholars is that the lesson lies in the general wording, not in the particular incident.

short: The gathering of the Qur'an into one written volume, carried out under Abu Bakr and then Uthman.
long: It was already written in the Prophet's lifetime on parchment, palm stalks and bone, and memorised by many Companions. After heavy losses among the reciters at the battle of Yamamah, Abu Bakr had Zayd ibn Thabit gather it into one set of sheets, which were later kept by Hafsah. Uthman then had standard copies made from those sheets and sent to the main cities, so that the whole community read from one text.

short: The spelling of the Uthmanic copies, kept in mushafs even where it differs from modern Arabic spelling.
long: The original copies carried no dots and no vowel marks, only the consonantal skeleton, which could hold more than one authentic reading at once. Later scholars added dots, vowels and stop marks without touching that skeleton. This is why some words are written in the mushaf differently from how they are written today, and why Uthmani and simplified Indo-Pak printings look unlike each other on the page.

short: The seven modes in which the Qur'an was revealed, an ease for the community; what a mode is stays disputed.
long: The Prophet said the Qur'an was sent down in seven ahruf, and the report appears in the most reliable collections. What an harf actually is has been argued over for centuries, with dozens of explanations offered and none settled. The ahruf are not the same thing as the ten qira'at, though the readings preserve part of what the ahruf allowed.

short: The canonical ways of reciting the Qur'an, each carried by chain from the Prophet through a named reader.
long: Ten readings are accepted as authentic, each passed on by two main transmitters, giving twenty transmissions in common use. The differences are small and mostly touch vowels, lengthening or a single letter; they rarely change meaning, and where they do the two meanings sit alongside each other rather than clash. A reading counts as authentic only if it has a sound chain, fits the Uthmanic skeleton and is valid Arabic.

short: The reading found in most printed mushafs today, transmitted by Hafs from his teacher Asim of Kufa.
long: Hafs ibn Sulayman learned it from Asim ibn Abi an-Najud, whose chain runs back through the Companions to the Prophet. It spread with mass printing and is now the default across most of the Muslim world, which is why many readers assume it is the only way the Qur'an is read. Asim's other transmitter, Shu'bah, differs from Hafs in a modest number of places.

short: The reading common in North and West Africa, transmitted by Warsh from Nafi of Madinah.
long: Uthman ibn Sa'id, nicknamed Warsh, took it from Nafi al-Madani, and it travelled west with the scholars of the Maghrib. Set beside Hafs it lengthens certain vowels further, handles some hamzahs more softly, and tilts some fathas towards a kasra. Nafi's other transmitter is Qalun, whose reading is used in Libya and parts of Tunisia.

short: A licence to teach a reading, granted after reciting the entire Qur'an to a qualified teacher.
long: The teacher listens to every letter, corrects it, and only then names the student in an unbroken chain of teachers reaching back to the Prophet. It certifies that you were heard, not that you passed a written exam. Most ijazahs given today are in Hafs from Asim, though teachers of the other readings still grant them.

short: The beginner's tajwid poem students memorise, alongside al-Jazariyyah and, for the readings, ash-Shatibiyyah.
long: Tuhfat al-Atfal, by al-Jamzuri, covers the rules of nun sakinah, meem sakinah and madd in about sixty lines of verse. Al-Jazariyyah, by Ibn al-Jazari, goes further into the articulation points and qualities of the letters. Ash-Shatibiyyah is the long poem behind the seven readings, and students normally reach it only after the first two are secure.

short: Abrogation: a later ruling replacing an earlier one, the abrogating verse and the abrogated verse.
long: The Qur'an raises the idea itself, and the clearest example is the change of qiblah from Jerusalem to the Kaaba. Early scholars listed hundreds of cases, often using the word loosely for any narrowing or qualifying of a general rule. Later scholars tightened the definition sharply, and Shah Waliullah held that only about five genuine cases remain; the count is still debated.

short: The clear verses whose meaning is decisive, and the verses that can carry more than one meaning.
long: The Qur'an draws the distinction itself, in Surah Al Imran, and warns against those who chase the ambiguous looking for discord. Muhkam verses are the backbone: the commands, the prohibitions, the plain statements. Mutashabih covers what is genuinely open to more than one reading, and matters of the unseen whose reality many scholars leave to Allah rather than forcing into a shape.

short: The study of how verses and surahs connect, and why they sit in the order they do.
long: It asks why one verse follows another, and how a surah opens and closes on the same note. Al-Biqa'i's Nazm ad-Durar is the largest classical work built entirely on this idea. Some early scholars were cautious about it, since the arrangement is a matter of revelation rather than an author ordering his chapters.

short: The study of the Qur'an's rare or difficult words, and what they meant to their first hearers.
long: Arabic shifts over time, and words that were everyday in the seventh century can be obscure now. Ibn Abbas is known for explaining such words by citing lines of pre Islamic poetry. Al-Raghib al-Isfahani's Mufradat is the standard reference and is still the first book a student opens on a hard word.

short: The parables of the Qur'an: everyday images used to make an unseen truth visible.
long: A spider's house for false reliance, a lamp in a niche for light upon light, ash scattered by the wind for deeds without faith. The Qur'an says it sets out such comparisons for people so that they may reflect. Reading them as pictures rather than as puzzles to decode is usually the point.

also: by the fig and the olive
short: The oaths of the Qur'an, where Allah swears by the dawn, the pen, the fig, the soul.
long: The oath usually points at what follows it, so the thing sworn by is a clue to the truth being affirmed. The Prophet taught that people may swear only by Allah, and this is no contradiction: the Creator may swear by whatever He has made. Ibn al-Qayyim's at-Tibyan is the classic study of the subject.

short: The Qur'an's inimitability: that no one can produce its like, and the standing challenge to try.
long: The challenge is made in stages within the Qur'an, from producing ten surahs like it down to a single surah, addressed to the finest speakers of a language that prized poetry above everything. Classical scholars located the miracle mainly in the arrangement and cadence of the Arabic, not only in what is said. Modern claims about scientific miracles are a separate and much more contested argument.

short: Explanation of the Qur'an: what a verse means, why it came, and what it asks of you.
long: The word means to uncover, the way you pull a cover off a thing. A tafsir works through the text verse by verse using the rest of the Qur'an, the Sunnah, the sayings of the Companions and the Arabic language. Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Razi are among the best known, and they differ in focus, so reading one is not reading them all.

short: A scholar who writes or teaches tafsir, trained in Arabic, the readings, the Sunnah and the occasions.
long: Classical scholars set a demanding bar here, since an error is an error about the speech of Allah. The one thing a mufassir may never do is state what a verse means on the strength of personal opinion alone. Any reader may reflect on the Qur'an; explaining it authoritatively to others is a trained job.

short: Tafsir built on transmitted reports, as against tafsir bi'r-ra'y, which reasons from language and principle.
long: Transmitted tafsir explains the Qur'an by the Qur'an, then by the Sunnah, then by the Companions and their students. Reasoned tafsir uses grammar, context and legal principle; it is praised when it is disciplined and condemned when it is a person reading their preferences into the text. Most of the great commentaries mix the two rather than holding to one.

short: Stories from earlier scriptures that entered tafsir to supply details the Qur'an deliberately leaves out.
long: The Qur'an tells its stories for their lesson, so names, dates and numbers are often absent, and early commentators sometimes reached for Jewish and Christian material to fill the gaps. The rule scholars settled on has three parts: accept what our own sources confirm, reject what they contradict, and neither affirm nor deny the rest. A good deal of what people repeat as Qur'anic detail is actually israiliyyat.

short: Interpretation, and in a second sense the reality a statement finally turns out to refer to.
long: Early scholars used ta'wil and tafsir almost interchangeably; Tabari's great commentary carries the word in its title. Later it came to mean moving a word away from its apparent sense on the strength of evidence, which is where much theological argument lives. In Shia and Sufi writing the word often carries a further sense, an inner meaning beneath the plain one, which Sunni scholars accept only where it does not cancel the plain meaning.

short: Slow reflection on the Qur'an, letting a verse work on you instead of passing over it.
long: The root means to look at the far end of a thing, to follow it to its outcome. The Qur'an names this as the purpose of its revelation and asks more than once whether people reflect on it at all. Tadabbur is not tafsir: it needs no training, only attention, honesty, and enough of the meaning to know what you are reading.

short: A translation of the Qur'an, properly called a translation of the meanings rather than the Qur'an itself.
long: No translation carries the Arabic wording, and every translator has already made interpretive choices, so a translation is really a compressed tafsir. This is why prayer is recited in Arabic; Abu Hanifah is reported to have allowed reciting the meaning in prayer, his two main students allowed it only for someone genuinely unable, and he is reported to have come round to their view. A translated volume is also not given the same rulings as a mushaf.

short: Reciting the Qur'an aloud, following its words closely rather than merely reading over them.
long: The root carries the sense of following, one word behind another, which is why the term implies obedience as well as recitation. The Qur'an praises those who recite it as it deserves to be recited. In practice tilawah is done with wudu where possible, at a measured pace, opening with the isti'adhah.

short: Reciting slowly and distinctly, giving every letter its right, as the Qur'an itself instructs.
long: The command is direct: and recite the Qur'an with tartil. Ali is reported to have explained it as giving the letters their due and knowing where to stop. It was the Prophet's own pace, and it is the one to use if you want to understand what you are saying.

short: The middle speed of recitation, sitting between the slow tartil and the quick hadr.
long: It keeps every rule of tajwid fully in place while moving at a working pace. This is how most imams recite in tarawih and how most students revise. All three speeds are permitted; what is not permitted is speed that swallows letters.

short: Fast recitation that still keeps every rule intact, used mainly when revising memorisation.
long: Speed itself is allowed; dropping letters, cutting a madd short or blurring word endings is not. A hafiz revising several juz in a day will usually recite in hadr. If the words begin running into each other, the answer is to slow down rather than push on.

short: Two recorded styles: mujawwad is slow and ornamented for listening, murattal is even and plain.
long: Mujawwad is the style of the great reciters at public gatherings, with long pauses and phrases repeated at different pitches. Murattal moves steadily from beginning to end and is what most people use for daily listening and for memorising. Both must obey the same tajwid; the difference is delivery, not rules.

short: A reciter of the Qur'an; in the classical sense, one trained and certified in a particular reading.
long: The plural is qurra, and in the earliest generations it meant the scholars who carried the Qur'an rather than performers. A muqri is a qari licensed to teach and to grant ijazah. Today the word is used loosely for anyone who recites beautifully, which is harmless, but the older meaning is worth keeping in view.

short: The rules for pronouncing the Qur'an correctly: each letter from its place, with its proper qualities.
long: The word means to do a thing well. In practice it covers articulation points, letter qualities, lengthening, merging, hiding, and where to stop. Scholars broadly agree that learning enough to avoid errors that change meaning is required of every reciter; how much of the finer detail is obligatory is debated, and a beginner is not sinful for reciting imperfectly while learning.

short: The points in the mouth, throat and nose where each Arabic letter is produced.
long: Getting these right is what keeps letters apart, so that one throat letter does not slide into another, or sin into thaa. The most common count is seventeen points, grouped in the open air of the mouth, the throat, the tongue, the lips and the nose, though some early scholars counted sixteen or fourteen. They are learned out loud with a teacher, not from a diagram.

short: The qualities of each letter: whispered or voiced, heavy or light, tense or flowing.
long: Two letters can share one articulation point and still be different letters because their qualities differ, as with ta and da. Some qualities come in opposite pairs and some stand alone, like the whistle of sin or the roll of ra. Together with the makharij they are the two halves of pronouncing a letter correctly.

short: A nun carrying no vowel, or a tanwin ending, which triggers four tajwid rules depending on what follows.
long: Tanwin is the doubled vowel sign at the end of a word, sounded as an n. The letter that comes next decides what happens to it: izhar, idgham, iqlab or ikhfa. This single family of rules is where nearly every beginner's tajwid course starts.

short: Pronouncing a nun sakinah or tanwin clearly, with no nasal hum, before one of six throat letters.
long: The six are hamzah, ha, ayn, ha, ghayn and kha, all produced in the throat. Because the throat sits far from the nose, the nun is simply left as it is. There is a matching rule for a silent meem, called izhar shafawi, made at the lips.

short: Merging a nun sakinah or tanwin into the letter that follows, so the two are said as one.
long: The six letters are gathered in the word yarmaloon: ya, ra, meem, lam, waw and nun. With ya, nun, meem and waw the merge keeps a nasal hum; with lam and ra it does not. The term also covers any two identical or close letters running together, as when a word ending in dal meets a word beginning with dal.

short: Turning a nun sakinah or tanwin into a meem when the next letter is ba, held with a hum.
long: The lips come together lightly for the meem sound and the hum is held about two counts, without pressing the lips shut. Mushafs mark it with a small meem written above the nun or the tanwin. It happens with only one letter, ba, which makes it the easiest of the four rules to spot.

short: Hiding a nun sakinah or tanwin: not clear, not merged, held with a nasal hum for two counts.
long: It applies before fifteen letters, the ones left once the letters of izhar, idgham and iqlab are taken out. The tongue moves towards the position of the coming letter without quite touching, and the sound rests in the nose. There is a related lip rule, ikhfa shafawi, for a silent meem followed by ba.

short: The nasal hum carried by nun and meem, held about two counts wherever the rules require it.
long: It comes out through the nose, not the mouth: pinch your nose and the sound is cut off. It is fullest on a nun or meem carrying a shaddah, which is why those two are called the letters of ghunnah. It also appears inside idgham, ikhfa and iqlab.

short: The slight bounce on five letters when they carry no vowel: qaf, taa, ba, jim and dal.
long: Teachers gather them in the phrase qutbu jad. The bounce is small in the middle of a word and stronger when you stop on the letter at the end of a verse. It is a spring off the letter, not an added vowel, so no eh or uh sound should be heard after it.

short: Lengthening a vowel with alif, waw or ya, held for a set number of counts.
long: The natural madd is two counts and needs no sign in the text. Longer types are triggered by a hamzah or a sukun after the vowel and stretch to four, five or six counts depending on the type and the reading. Getting the count wrong can change a word entirely, which is why madd is drilled so hard.

short: Heavy and light pronunciation: some letters fill the mouth, others stay thin.
long: Seven letters are always heavy, gathered by teachers in a mnemonic phrase, khussa daghtin qiz. Ra and the lam in the name Allah switch between heavy and light depending on the vowels around them, and alif simply follows whatever came before it. The distinction is not decorative: a heavy letter said thin can turn one word into a different word.

short: Tilting a fatha towards a kasra, so the vowel lands somewhere between an a and an e.
long: It belongs to some readings far more than others; Warsh uses a lighter form of it, called taqlil, in many places. In the Hafs reading there is one clear case, in the word majreha in Surah Hud. It is a transmitted pronunciation, not a regional accent or a matter of taste.

short: Where you stop while reciting, and where you may not, shown by small letters above the line.
long: The familiar marks come from a system worked out by later scholars rather than from revelation: meem means stop, la means do not stop here, jeem means you may, and paired sets of three dots mean stop at one of the two but not both. Stopping in the wrong place can break the sense of a sentence, which is why the marks were added at all. The same word waqf also means a charitable endowment, an entirely separate subject.

short: A brief silence held without taking a breath, then the recitation carries straight on.
long: It keeps two words from running together in a way that could mislead the ear. In the Hafs reading there are four of them, in al-Kahf, Ya-Sin, al-Qiyamah and al-Mutaffifin, and the mushaf marks each with a small seen. Other readings place their pauses differently.

short: A mistake in recitation: the clear kind changes letters or vowels, the hidden kind breaks finer rules.
long: Lahn jali means mispronouncing a letter or a case ending, and because it can change the meaning, scholars treat correcting it as an obligation. Lahn khafi means shortening a madd, missing a ghunnah and the like, a matter of polish rather than sin. Everyone makes both while learning; the remedy is to recite to someone who can hear them.

short: Memorising the Qur'an by heart, traditionally with a teacher who hears you every day.
long: The word means preservation, the same word the Qur'an uses when it says Allah has taken the preservation of this revelation upon Himself. Memorisation has been the main way that happened: in every generation enough people carried the whole text that no copy could quietly go missing. A memoriser adds a small portion each day and spends far more time revising than adding.

short: Someone who has memorised the whole Qur'an and can recite it from memory.
long: The plural is huffaz and the feminine is hafizah. In the hadith sciences the same title means a scholar who has memorised a vast number of narrations, so it is not always about the Qur'an. It is not a permanent state either: without revision it slips away, which is why huffaz keep reciting for life.

short: Revision of what you have memorised, the daily work that keeps the Qur'an from slipping away.
long: The Prophet compared memorised Qur'an to tethered camels: let go of the rope and they are gone. Traditional schools split the day into new memorisation, recent revision and old revision, called sabaq, sabqi and manzil in South Asian madrasas. Most people who lose their hifz lose it here rather than in the memorising.

short: Completing a full reading of the Qur'an from beginning to end.
long: Many aim for one in Ramadan at a juz a day, and most mosques finish the whole text across the nights of tarawih. The Prophet told a Companion who wanted to read faster not to complete it in fewer than three days, because understanding suffers. The supplication read at the end is a widespread custom rather than a fixed text from the Sunnah.

short: The prostration made on reaching one of the Qur'an's marked verses of prostration, in prayer or outside it.
long: The mushaf marks these verses in the margin, usually with the word sajdah and a line above the text. The schools count them differently, at eleven, fourteen or fifteen, so mushafs printed in different regions mark a different number of them. It is a single prostration, and most scholars hold it is recommended rather than required, including for someone who is only listening.

short: Whether wudu is needed to hold a copy of the Qur'an; the four schools say yes, a minority disagrees.
long: The four Sunni schools require purity to touch the mushaf itself, citing a verse in Surah al-Waqi'ah and the Prophet's letter to the people of Yemen; Ibn Hazm and others read that verse as speaking about the angels instead. Reciting from memory without wudu is agreed to be fine. Most contemporary scholars hold that a phone or tablet is not a mushaf, so the ruling does not extend to reading from a screen.
